messages.body_plain:
Sorry for any cross-posting. Note that the conference this year is in March rather than in April.  Also, this year's multilevel conference immediately precedes the Meeting of the SEM Working Group:  https://www.utwente.nl/en/et/dpm/chair/pmr/semg/

SAVE THE DATE and Call for Abstracts: The International Conference on Multilevel Analysis

The 14th International Multilevel Conference will be held on March 12-13, 2024.

The conference will be about all aspects of statistical multilevel analysis: innovative applications, theory, software, and methodology. The conference will be in an informal style, with much room for discussion. It will be held in the city centre of Utrecht, within a quarter hour walk or a five-minute bus ride from the Central railway station.

Keynote speakers include dr. Mirjam Moerbeek on sample size calculations and professor Dan McNeish on measurement in intensive longitudinal data. A first pre-conference workshop on extracting personalised latent dynamics using multilevel HMMs is taught by dr. Emmeke Aarts and a second pre-conference workshop on projection predictive variable selection is taught by Dr. Andrew Johnson

Abstract submission

Deadlines for submitting an abstract: If you submit before the 1st of November (2023), you will be notified on the 15th of November if your abstract is accepted. If you submit before the 7th of January (2024), you will be notified on the 21st of January if your abstract is accepted.

This edition of the conference will also have the option for researchers working with empirical data to submit posters with questions about their analyses or sampling design. During the conference you will have the opportunity to receive feedback on your (ongoing) research.

Young Researcher Award

The abstracts of four PhD students will be selected and these PhD students will be invited to present their work in a special symposium. The best presentation will be awarded during the closing ceremony with the 'Best PhD Multilevel Presentation Award' and their conference fee will be reimbursed.

Pre-conference workshops

There will be two pre-conference workshop(s) on March 11th. One of these is a workshop on extracting personalised latent dynamics using multilevel HMMs is taught by dr. Emmeke Aarts. A hands-on workshop on projection predictive variable selection for multilevel models using the R-package projpred will be taught by Dr. Andrew Johnson. Andrew will introduce the motivations behind and benefits of projection predictive selection, with an emphasis on practical application and real-world problems. Andrew is a postdoc with Aki Vehtari's group at Aalto University (Helsinki), who are the primary developers and maintainers of the projpred package. Andrew is also part of the development team for Stan, the increasingly popular program for Bayesian analysis.

The conference website with further information on abstract submission can be found at http://multilevel.fss.uu.nl/ <https://eur04.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=http%3A%2F%2Fmultilevel.fss.uu.nl%2F&data=05%...%40uva.nl%7C8e6872fa97d64f76abc608dbd6d33bcd%7Ca0f1cacd618c4403b94576fb3d6874e5%7C0%7C0%7C638339974972137719%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJWIjoiMC4wLjAwMDAiLCJQIjoiV2luMzIiLCJBTiI6Ik1haWwiLCJXVCI6Mn0%3D%7C3000%7C%7C%7C&sdata=5W18vgiltbYZKLvJxYngFpHD0juv2OOeCchmaaDX4g4%3D&reserved=0>

messages.subject: Re: Running time for different parameterization methods
messages.subject_clean: Running time for different parameterization methods
messages.body_plain:
> 67 items in the model. When we run the model with theta parameterization it takes a very long time to complete. When we run the model with delta parameterization it is somewhat faster, but still takes a couple of hours.

With so many ordinal variables, that is no surprise.  Inverting such a large weight matrix is computationally intensive.

> the wisdom seems to be to go with theta parameterization.

What wisdom?  If you are not explicitly testing hypotheses about constraints on residual variances, then the 2 parameterizations are statistically equivalent.  The Mplus documentation noted long ago that the delta is more stable, likely because residual variances can be negative (often to to sampling error, but with your very large sample, it could be a sign of misspecification).  If you have a negative residual variance using delta, then that would obviously create a problem for an optimizer looking for a solution that fixes the residual variance to 1 using theta.

Speed is less virtuous than validity of results, but you could try analyzing your data as continuous, if there are several categories (or even if not: Robitzsch, 2020 <https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2020.589965>).  It's a matter of choosing one set of unlikely assumptions over another.  At least when treating as continuous, you can adjust for nonnormality.  If latent responses are not normal, there is no correction for that.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Fit meausures using sam function with multiple imputation (mitml)
messages.subject_clean: Fit meausures using sam function with multiple imputation (mitml)
messages.body_plain:
> 1) Because of the nature of the items and each item has only one correct answer I created 27 dummy variables to analyze the data in the sem models. Is this approach correct or do I have to use the 30 original items? All 27 dummy items are categorical, most of them are binary (0 if wrong and 1 if right, but only 6 items have three values (0, 0.5 and 1) because the 3 pairs of items were dependent in the sense of partial credit approach.

If "partially correct" is a category between "not at all correct" and "fully correct", then you need to have a single ordinal variable coded that way.  The numerical values are arbitrary, as long as the order is recognized by lavaan.  You could use the ordered() function to make the levels explicit.

> 2) My sample size is small (149) and missing data is around 5%, so I wonder if is necessary to use multiple imputations here (I tested the original 30 items and Little's MCAR test reject, but when using the 27 dummy items, the same test is not significant) or pairwise would be enough.

MCAR is the null hypothesis.  It can be falsified by the data, but failing to reject is an inconclusive result.  There is no way to "verify" MCAR.  Imputation is often the most flexible way to include as many potentially informative auxiliary variables in your data to help justify the MAR assumption.  But there is nothing wrong with a sensitivity analysis, if you want to compare using missing="pairwise", potentially with estimator="PML".

> 3)  I couldn't obtain the fit measures for the model fit2_cb.sam

The chi-squared for SAM is a "pseudo" statistic that treats the "stage 1" saturated factor covariances as known.  As the article states (see ?sam References), the purpose of SAM is to make parameter estimation a bit more efficient, not to test model fit.

> I tried also the semTools package, but it only allowed me to use sem.Mi () function

I have not written a sam.mi() wrapper, nor do I intend to.  (A valid implementation would do all the pooling of the measurement results, then fit the structural model to the pooled latent covariance matrix.  But that has not been developed, and many details would need to be worked out first.)

I would recommend doing what you already did with mitml on fitted sam() results.  Just focus on pooled estimates, not the fit (pseudo)statistic.  Again, you could compare results to pairwise deletion as a sensitivity analysis.  If parameter estimates and SEs are similar, you could perhaps trust the fit statistic using pairwise deletion.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Replications not convergent
messages.subject_clean: Replications not convergent
messages.body_plain:
The design matrix calculates the interaction XW prior to setting X's actual (Likert-scale?) values of 1-5. So XW simply = W, which expect would not allow your model to converge because the sample covariance matrix would not be positive definite if 2 predictors are perfectly correlated.

Since you have a Likert-scale predictor, I would recommend you think more carefully about the response distribution you expect (which seems random, not fixed, invalidating the exogeneity assumption of your simulation.)  If you really think that the distribution of X is fixed (i.e., has specific probabilities for each response option), you should first generate a sample of minimal size with that property.  For example, assuming something normalish looking:

(X <- rep(1:5, times = c(.1, .2, .4, .2, .1)*10))
W <- 1:0
expand.grid(X, W)

That leads to orthogonal X and W, then you create their interaction term XW.  That basic building block (here, 20 observations) can be repeated however often to yield samples of different sizes following that fixed design (e.g., 5 of those yield N = 100).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Test of Group Invariance with 3 Groups
messages.subject_clean: Test of Group Invariance with 3 Groups
messages.body_plain:
Dear Terrence
Thanks a lot for your prompt reply and your willingness to give a hand in this problem. The three groups are coded with names, so, the group ordering in the dataset was done alphabetically.
The first groups was called "Aut", the second "Com" and the third "Rel". So, it was "Aut" (the first group, alphabetically ordered) which was compared to "Com" (the second group) and "Rel" (the third group). So, what lavaan does is to get the first group that it finds in the dataset (the "Aut" group) and compare it with the other two.
To override the ordering, and make the "Com" appear first in the group I used the following commands
df$newfactor <- factor(df$oldfactor, levels = c('Com', 'Aut', 'Rel'))
dfNew <- <- df[order(df$newfactor), ]

So the dfNew has ordered the same data with the "Com"  group being the first, and thus the reference group.
So, what I did in the next step was to rerun the lavaan model with the dfNew .

A. Test of group invariance with "Aut" being the reference group with df data frame

Part of the lavTestScore

B. Test of group invariance with "Com" being the reference group using the dfNew data frame

Part of the lavTestScore with the reordered group
Same chi-square but the x2 of the first group (Com) with the second group (Aut) now differs.
Instead, the comparison between the first group (Com) with third group (Rel) gives the same chi-square with the previously first group (Aut) with the third one (Rel).

As for the "group.label", I did not know that function. At any rate, it gives the same results with my own (less-clear) way of regrouping.
Kind regards
Athanasios Mouratidis

messages.subject: Unequal time coding and convergence errors
messages.subject_clean: Unequal time coding and convergence errors
messages.body_plain:
Dear Lavaan Users,

We are fitting a cubic growth model as follows and have unequal time points, so have adjusted as necessary. Given the large magnitude of the fixed coefficients of growth functions, this seems to be causing some convergence issues (Hessian Matrix errors as estimates close to zero) as the other estimated parameters (particularly variance terms) are particularly small.

model <- ' i =~ 1*t1 + 1*t2 + 1*t3 + 1*t4  + 1*t5 + 1*t6     <https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/growth.html#cb2-2> s =~ 0*t1 + 2*t2 + 4*t3 + 8*t4 + 11*t5 + 14*t6
q =~ 0*t1 + 4*t2 + 16*t3 + 64*t4 + 121*t5 + 196*t6
c =~ 0*t1 + 16*t2 + 64*t3 + 512*t4 + 1331*t5 + 2744*t6 '
To compensate, we have reduced the model proportionately, so that the spacing remains proportionately correct but the overall magnitude is much smaller. This seems to avoid this issue as variance estimates are no longer near zero.

model <- ' i =~ 1*t1 + 1*t2 + 1*t3 + 1*t4  + 1*t5 + 1*t6     <https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/growth.html#cb2-2> s =~ 0*t1 + 1*t2 + 2*t3 + 4*t4 + 5.5*t5 + 7*t6
q =~ 0*t1 + 1*t2 + 4*t3 + 16*t4 + 30.25*t5 + 49*t6
c =~ 0*t1 + 1*t2 + 16*t3 + 64*t4 + 166.38*t5 + 343*t6 '

Is this strategy sensible or is there a better option please? Thanks in advance for any advise offered.

messages.subject: Re: Unequal time coding and convergence errors
messages.subject_clean: Unequal time coding and convergence errors
messages.body_plain:
Orthogonal polynomial contrasts should help:

https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1027/1614-2241/a000044

The R function contr.poly() is flexible, accepting a vector of “time” scores in case measurements are unequally spaced. It provides orthonormal contrasts, which are not only orthogonal but are scaled to each have SD=1.

Best,
Terrence Jorgensen

messages.subject_clean: Problems with fitting a Latent Growth Curve Model with a Grouped Time-varying covariate in R
messages.body_plain:
Hi all!

I am new to lavaan and longitudinal data analysis and I have trouble fitting a Latent Growth Curve Model with a Time-varying covariate in R. In my research (Youtube, forums, etc.) I figured that this kind of model would be most suitable due to my datas properties:
- Longitudinal, balanced and continuous data with 11 time points
- The longitudinal data is autocorrelated (some of the data is more or less linear, the other is growing S-shaped)
- 79 of such time series that are from two groups which I want to compare. Does the growth of group B influence the growth of goup A? Group A is mostly stagnant growth, group B is the "newcomers" that might or might not take away from the other group.

So far, I have transformed the data in the wide format:

Name Grouping  t1 t2 t... t11
Slope 1 Group A 2.1 2.2 ... ...
Slope 2 Group A 10.4 9.5 ... ...
Slope 3 Group B 0.1 1 ... ...
Slope 4 Group B 0.5 5 ... ...
Slope ... Group ... ... ... ... ...
Slope 79  Group A 100.4 110.0 ... ...

I have not really managed to determine the fitting. According to the manuel (https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/growth.html) it would look something like:

# Define the lavaan growth model
model = "
    # intercept and slope with fixed coefficients
    inter =~ 1*t1 + 1*t2 + 1*t3 + 1*t4 + 1*t5 + 1*t6 + 1*t7 + 1*t8 + 1*t9 + 1*t10 + 1*t11
    slope =~ 0*t1 + 1*t2 + 2*t3 + 3*t4 + 4*t5 + 5*t6 + 6*t7 + 7*t8 + 8*t9 + 9*t10 + 10*t11
    # regressions
    i ~ x1 + x2
    s ~ x1 + x2
   # time-varying covariates
    t1 ~ c1
    t2 ~ c2
    t3 ~ c3
    t4 ~ c4
    t5 ~ c5
    t6 ~ c6
    t7 ~ c7
    t8 ~ c8
    t9 ~ c9
    t10 ~ c10
    t11 ~ c11
'
fit <- growth(model, data = filtered_data_wide)
summary(fit)

Now I am not sure how to fit the multi-level structure according to my question, i.e. does Group B influence the Growth of group A (Group A vs. B): https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/multilevel.html. I have also looked here (- https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/uZgXzgBoEKA?pli=1) and here (https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/uZgXzgBoEKA?pli=1), but they seem to do slightly different things.

I would be more than happy if anyone could help or give hints. I am really desperate how to proceed.

Many thanks in advance!
Michael

My multigroup confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) confirms weak invariance but not strong scalar invariance. Based on this, I believe I can compare the covariance structures across countries, but not the mean structures, in line with what I've learned from the literature.

1) Does this allow me to proceed with a multigroup structural equation modeling (SEM) where I can examine and contrast the regression coefficients, but not the latent means, across the different groups?

2) If weak invariance is not established, does it mean I can conduct separate SEMs for each country and qualitatively discuss their outcomes? Can I compare the conceptual implications of the findings, acknowledging that a quantitative comparison of the latent means is not valid?

Thank you!
Sara

messages.subject: Structural Equation Model Not Finding a Solution/Converging
messages.subject_clean: Structural Equation Model Not Finding a Solution/Converging
messages.body_plain:
Hello, I am currently trying to fit a Structural Equation Model using lavaan to data that I have simulated, and am having issues with model convergence. I have attached a png of the path diagram for the model to this discussion. Forgive me if it is slightly hard to read, I was not very familiar with the software I used to generate it. My goal in fitting this model is to estimate the factor loading matrices. I want to accurately estimate the factor loading matrices (which are known as I use them to simulate the data), and to do so, I impose several constraints such that there is no indeterminancy (rotational, scalar, or otherwise). The constraints, as seen in the path diagram, are as follows:

1. For the factor loadings between my observed independent covariates (X1-X20) and the latent factors from which they are generated (W1-W3), I have fixed the factor loadings for X1~W1, X2~W2, and X3~W3 at 1, and the factor loadings for X1~W2, X1~W3, and X2~W3 at 0.

2. For the factor loadings between my observed dependent covariates (Y1-Y20) and the latent factors from which they are generated (Z1-Z2), I have fixed the factor loadings for Y1~Z1, and Y2~Z2 at 1, and the factor loading for Y1~Z2 at 0.

3. The 3 latent factors W1, W2, and W3 have variance 1, and all 3 are mutually independent.

To the best of my knowledge, these should be sufficient conditions such that the remaining (unfixed) factor loadings between (X1-X20) and (W1-W3), (Y1-Y20) and (Z1-Z2), and coefficient matrix containing the regression estimates of (Z1-Z2) on (W1-W3) can all be uniquely estimated. Of course, the true factor loadings and covariance matrix of (W1-W3) are correspondingly fixed at these values. The covariance matrices of the error terms (which are simply the identity matrix) should be estimable as well, though these are not of particular interest currently. However, when I try and fit this model as I have defined it in lavaan, I receive a warning message from the optimizer stating that a solution has not been found, and correspondingly, the estimated factor loadings and regression coefficients are quite inaccurate. I have found that when I fix a single one of the regression coefficients of (Z1-Z2) on (W1-W3) at the truth (it does not seem to matter which coefficient I choose), I receive no warnings or errors when fitting the model, and the estimated factor loadings and regression coefficients are accurate. Is anyone able to help me figure out why these issues are arising when fitting the model? I have also included below the R code I have used to define and fit my model. Please let me know if any further clarifications are desired. Thank you very much for the assistance.

Best,

Alexander

library(lavaan)
library(stringr)

datgen <- function(ak, bk, gamma, n,varvecB,varvecA,varvecG){
  if((is.atomic(gamma)) & (length(gamma) == 1L)){
    W <- matrix(rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1), nrow = 1, n)
  }
  else{
    W <- matrix(rnorm(n*ncol(gamma), mean = 0, sd = 1), nrow = ncol(gamma), n) ## generate matrix U N(0,I) m x n
  }
  xlin.term  <-  bk %*% rbind(rep(1, ncol(W)),W)
  xlin.term <- t(xlin.term)
  xx <- matrix(0, nrow = n, ncol = nrow(bk))
  for(jj in 1: (ncol(xx))){
    xx[, jj] <- xlin.term[,jj] + cbind(rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = sqrt(varvecB[jj])))
  }
  colnames(xlin.term) <- paste0('X', 1:(ncol(xx)))
  colnames(xx) <- paste0('X', 1:(ncol(xx)))
  X = xx

  if((is.atomic(gamma)) & (length(gamma) == 1L)){
    Z <- gamma*W + matrix(rnorm(n, mean = 0, sqrt(varvecG)), nrow = 1) ## generate latent matrix Z
  }
  else{
    Z <- matrix(0, nrow=nrow(gamma), ncol = n)
    for(i in 1:nrow(gamma)){
      Z[i,] <- gamma[i,]%*%W + matrix(rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = sqrt(varvecG[i])), nrow = 1) ## generate latent matrix Z
    }
  }
  ylin.term  <-  ak %*% rbind(rep(1, ncol(Z)),Z)
  ylin.term <- t(ylin.term)
  yy <- matrix(0, nrow = n, ncol = nrow(ak))
  for(jj in 1: (ncol(yy))){
    yy[, jj] <- ylin.term[,jj] + cbind(rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = sqrt(varvecA[jj])))
  }
  colnames(ylin.term) <- paste0('Y', 1:(ncol(yy)))
  colnames(yy) <- paste0('Y', 1:(ncol(yy)))
  Y = yy
  output <- list("X" = X, "Y" = Y, "Z" = Z)
}

set.seed(2435)

paramsA0 <- rnorm(20)
paramsB0 <- rnorm(20)
paramsB <- matrix(c(1, -0.65, 0.65, rep(0.8,7), rep(0.70, 10), 0, 1, 0.70, rep(-0.85, 7), rep(-0.75, 10), 0, 0, 1, rep(0.55, 7), rep(-0.85, 10)), nrow = 20, ncol = 3)
paramsA <- matrix(c(1, 0.45, -0.80, rep(0.80, 7), rep(-0.45, 10), 0, 1, 0.70, rep(0.40, 7), rep(-0.95, 10)), nrow = 20, ncol = 2)
paramsG <- matrix(c(0.60, -0.75, -0.70, 0.65, 0.80, -0.55), nrow = 2, ncol = 3)
q <- 20
p <- 20
s <- 3
m <- 2

paramsAstotal <- cbind(paramsA0, paramsA)
paramsBstotal <- cbind(paramsB0, paramsB)

varvecB <- rep(1,20)
varvecA <- rep(1,20)
varvecG <- rep(1,m)

set.seed(1)

dat <- datgen(paramsAstotal, paramsBstotal, paramsG, 200, varvecB, varvecA, varvecG)

colnames(dat$X) <- sprintf("X%d", 1:q)
colnames(dat$Y) <- sprintf("Y%d", 1:p)

mydat <- cbind(dat$X, dat$Y)

X1vals <- substr(paste(sprintf("x%d*X%d +", 1:q, 1:q), collapse = ' '), 1 ,nchar(paste(sprintf("x%d*X%d +", 1:q, 1:q), collapse = ' '))  - 2)
X2vals <- substr(paste(sprintf("x%d*X%d +", (q+1):(2*q), 1:q), collapse = ' '), 1 ,nchar(paste(sprintf("x%d*X%d +", (q+1):(2*q), 1:q), collapse = ' '))  - 2)
X3vals <- substr(paste(sprintf("x%d*X%d +", (2*q+1):(3*q), 1:q), collapse = ' '), 1 ,nchar(paste(sprintf("x%d*X%d +", (2*q+1):(3*q), 1:q), collapse = ' '))  - 2)
Y1vals <- substr(paste(sprintf("y%d*Y%d +", 1:p, 1:p), collapse = ' '), 1 ,nchar(paste(sprintf("y%d*Y%d +", 1:p, 1:p), collapse = ' '))  - 2)
Y2vals <- substr(paste(sprintf("y%d*Y%d +", (p+1):(2*p), 1:p), collapse = ' '), 1 ,nchar(paste(sprintf("y%d*Y%d +", (p+1):(2*p), 1:p), collapse = ' '))  - 2)
Wvals <- substr(paste(sprintf("w%d*W%d +", 1:s, 1:s), collapse = ' '), 1 ,nchar(paste(sprintf("w%d*W%d +", 1:s, 1:s), collapse = ' '))  - 2)
X1model <- paste(paste0(sprintf("W%d =~ ", 1), X1vals), sep = '\n')
X2model <- paste(paste0(sprintf("W%d =~ ", 2), X2vals), sep = '\n')
X3model <- paste(paste0(sprintf("W%d =~ ", 3), X3vals), sep = '\n')
Y1model <- paste(paste0(sprintf("Z%d =~ ", 1), Y1vals), sep = '\n')
Y2model <- paste(paste0(sprintf("Z%d =~ ", 2), Y2vals), sep = '\n')
Xmodel <- c(X1model, X2model, X3model)

Wcov <- c()

k <- 1

for(i in 1:s){
  Xmodel[i] <- gsub(paste0("x", i+q*(i-1), "[*]X", i, " "), paste0("1*X", i, " "), Xmodel[i])
  for(j in 1:s){
    if(i < j){
      Wcov[k] <- paste(sprintf("W%d ~~ 0*W%d", i, j), sep = '\n')
      k <- k+1
    }
  }
}
Xmodel[2] <- gsub(paste0("x21"), paste0("0"), Xmodel[2])
Xmodel[3] <- gsub(paste0("x41"), paste0("0"), Xmodel[3])
Xmodel[3] <- gsub(paste0("x42"), paste0("0"), Xmodel[3])

for(i in 1:m){
  Ymodel[i] <- gsub(paste0("y", i+p*(i-1), "[*]Y", i, " "), paste0("1*Y", i, " "), Ymodel[i])
}
Ymodel[2] <- gsub(paste0("y21"), paste0("0"), Ymodel[2])
Zmodel <- c("Z1 ~ W1 + W2 + W3", "Z2 ~ W1 + W2 + W3")

#below is code where 1 of the regression coefficients is fixed at the truth
#Zmodel <- c("Z1 ~ W1 + W2 + W3", "Z2 ~ W1 + W2 + -0.55*W3")

mymodel <- c(Xmodel, Ymodel, Zmodel, Wvar, Wcov)
lav_mod <- sem(mymodel, data = mydat, meanstructure = T)

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Just chiming in a little late because I am currently experiencing the same issue, and am suspecting that it has to do with the ordered() function.
I am using the data from example 1 from the '"Structural-After-Measurement" (SAM) approach to SEM' paper <https://osf.io/w9bmf> by Rosseel & Loh (2022) and their OSF page. <https://osf.io/pekbm/>
I used the same model as given in the example and accompanying R script, which is as follows:

model <- '
  # measurement part
    ost   =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
    self  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
    other =~ x4 + x5 + x6
  # structural part
    ost   ~ b1*self + b2*other + c*sol + age + gender
    self  ~ a1*sol + age + gender
    other ~ a2*sol + age + gender
  # residual correlations
    self ~~ other '

I used the same syntax for fitting the model, except that I specified the indicators as ordered (and removed the 'estimator = "ML"', since I expected the estimator to become "WLSMV"):

fit.lsam_o <- sam(model, data = Data, sam.method = "local", ordered = c("x1", "x2", "x3", "x4", "x5", "x6", "y1", "y2", "y3", "y4"))
summary(fit.lsam_o)

I receive the same error as Jesse: Error in Mg %*% COV : requires numeric/complex matrix/vector arguments

Changing the variable structure in the dataset to be ordered (using as.ordered), or simply specifying "ordered = TRUE" in the syntax, did not help. Running the model without the ordered() function does work. Omitting the ordered part in the syntax but setting the estimator to "WLSMV" does work — but I am not sure whether this really treats the indicators as categorical.

Although the Rosseel & Loh (2022) paper states that "we will focus on settings where all latent variables and their indicators are continuous", I wonder whether it might still be possible to run the model with ordered indicators? The study I will be running has Likert-scale items, which are ordinal. It would be great if it were possible to respect the ordinal nature of Likert-scale items while running a SAM.

Or is there perhaps another reason for this error that has nothing to do with the ordered() function?

Thanks very much in advance,

Kind regards,
Floor Burghoorn

messages.body_plain:
Sara--
1. Yes. The covariance structure model and mean structure model are essentially independent, except in special circumstances.
2. You obviously can run the analysis. You will have results for several national samples. You could make statements about fit within each sample. But you would not be justified in comparing parameter estimates across samples. It would be as if you are using a different number system for each country.

messages.subject: Re: Model identification
messages.subject_clean: Model identification
messages.body_plain:
Nicole
there are other causes for not positive definite beside high inter-correlations.
Perhaps there is an item with negative error variance within your model that is causing problems.
the sample size should be ok in that your case to variable ratio is greater than 5:1
Perhaps you should test each factor separately before merging them into one model.

here are some references you could consult for alternative causes and solutions.
Chen, F., Bollen, K. A., Paxton, P., Curran, P. J., & Kirby, J. B. (2001). Improper solutions in structural equation models: Causes, consequences, and strategies. Sociological Methods & Research, 29(4), 468-508. https://doi.org/10.1177/0049124101029004003
Dillon, W. R., Kumar, A., & Mulani, N. (1987). Offending estimates in covariance structure analysis: Comments on the causes of and solutions to Heywood cases. Psychological Bulletin, 101(1), 126-135.
Gerbing, D. W., & Anderson, J. C. (1987). Improper solutions in the analysis of covariance structures: Their interpretability and a comparison of alternate respecifications. Psychometrika, 52(1), 99-111. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02293958
Kolenikov, S., & Bollen, K. A. (2012). Testing Negative Error Variances: Is a Heywood Case a Symptom of Misspecification? Sociological Methods & Research, 41, 124-167. https://doi.org/10.1177/0049124112442138

messages.subject: Re: Multigroup Mediation Model
messages.subject_clean: Multigroup Mediation Model
messages.body_plain:
It's not an error, it's a warning.

It's not saying there is something wrong. It's saying that what you did might be OK, but maybe you should make sure it is OK.

When you write:

    stress ~ b11*practice + b12*style + c11*enrich + c12*conflict

You are saying to Lavaan that you want the parameter for
stress ~ practice
To be called b11 and to be equal in both groups.  Lavaan thinks that's unusual and suggests that you might want them to be different (because you can always constrain them to be equal if you want to).

To do this, you need two labels. I don't know what your countries are, but if they were Yemen and Zambia, then you could write:

    stress ~ c(y_b11, z_b11) *practice + c(y_b12, z_b12) *style + c(y_c11, z_c11) * enrich + c(y_c12, z_c12) *conflict

Now you have a separate parameter for each country.

Jeremy

messages.subject_clean: Fixed Effects with latent variables in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
> I wondered if anyone had any references or could confirm that fixed effect models can be used in a latent variable framework

Muthen (2002) describes the Mplus model here:

https://doi.org/10.2333/bhmk.29.81

But lavaan does not have separate matrices kappa/gamma for fixed effects on observed/latent variables.  Instead, exogenous variable(s) are internally "promoted" as single-indcator error-free latent predictor(s) of the same variable name(s).  You can see this approach reflected in the parameter matrices when you lavInspect(fit, "est").

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: clustering and attrition weights in Lavaan
messages.subject_clean: clustering and attrition weights in Lavaan
messages.body_plain:
On 11/10/23 15:29, Sreemanjari Kandhasamy wrote:
>  1. The Lavaan package description mentions that sampling.weights

>     argument is currently available only for the un-clustered data.

Indeed.

>     how should you account for attrition weights and cluster at the same
>     time in growth function of lavaan package?

If you use the 'clustered' (but not the multilevel) approach, then the
point estimates ignore the clustering anyway. So you can use the
sampling.weights to get point estimates.

To get standard errors, things are a bit tricky. Usually I would say:
use the bootstrap, but you need to take the clustering into account. One
approach is the 'resample' the clusters, and keep the units within a
cluster together.

>  2. Can Lavaan.survey package be used here?

I believe so. The svydesign() function from the survey package accepts
weights. So this should work.

(BTW, the lavaan.survey package is no longer maintained, but you can get
it from the CRAN archive).

Yves.

messages.subject: Extract df from an under-identified model
messages.subject_clean: Extract df from an under-identified model
messages.body_plain:
Is it possible to extract the degrees of freedom from an under-identified model (that has more parameters than known values). That is, I'd like to extract the df even when the df is negative. As a teaching exercise, I'm fitting a formative model and would like to demonstrate that additional constraints are required to make the model identifiable.

The model fit output shows the negative degrees of freedom:

```
> formativeModelFit lavaan 0.6.16 ended normally after 1 iteration Estimator ML Optimization method NLMINB Number of model parameters 5 Used Total Number of observations 44 75 Number of missing patterns 1 Model Test User Model: Test statistic NA Degrees of freedom -5 P-value (Unknown) NA
```

However, when I try to extract the df using the fitMeasures() function, here is what I get:

```
> fitMeasures(formativeModelFit, "df") numeric(0)
```

Here is the output of the fitMeasures() command when not specifying "df":

```
> fitMeasures(formativeModelFit) Error in if (!is.finite(X2) || !is.finite(df) || !is.finite(X2.null) || : missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed In addition: Warning messages: 1: In lav_partable_check(lavpartable, categorical = lavoptions$.categorical, : lavaan WARNING: automatically added intercepts are set to zero: [formative] 2: In lav_fit_cfi_lavobject(lavobject = object, fit.measures = fit.measures, : lavaan WARNING: computation of robust CFI failed.
```

messages.subject: SEM for fertility
messages.subject_clean: SEM for fertility
messages.body_plain:
I have been having sleepless nights fitting this SEM model. One of the objectives to be achieved is to determine if social economic status (SES) has a direct impact on the fertility level of reproductive-aged women.
The following are the variables of interest: Total children ever born (TCEB), fertility preference (fertility), Wealth index, educational level, place of residence, ideal number of children, contraceptive use, religion, age at first birth, age at first cohabitation, number of living children (living), region, age at first sex (sex), and marital status. (See attached file).

Below was how I developed the model but was producing error. Kindly assist on how to sort this syntax.

myModel <- ' # regressions
      TCEB+Fertility ~ SES+Demographic_Factors+Geo_Cultural_Factors+Ideal+Contraceptive
      SES ~ Reproductive_Behavior+Demographic_Factors
      Reproductive_Behavior ~ Demographic_Factors+Ideal

             # latent variable definitions
# Measurement Model for SES (Latent Variable 1)
    SES =~ Wealth+Education+Residence

  # Measurement Model for Reproductive Behavior (Latent Variable 2)
    Reproductive_Behavior =~ TCEB+Fertility+Ideal+Contraceptive

  # Measurement Model for Demographic Factors (Latent Variable 3)
    Demographic_Factors =~ Cohabitation+Birth+Age

  # Measurement Model for Geographic and Cultural Factors (Latent Variable 5)
    Geo_Cultural_Factors =~ Region+Religion+Marital

             # variances and covariances
    SES ~~ Reproductive_Behavior
    SES ~~ Demographic_Factors
    Reproductive_Behavior ~~ Demographic_Factors
    TCEB ~~ Fertility
    Reproductive_Behavior ~~ Geo_Cultural_Factors
    Demographic_Factors ~~ Geo_Cultural_Factors

             # intercepts
               TCEB ~ 1
               SES ~ 1
           '

messages.body_plain:
Thank you for your reply; very much appreciated.
The assumption of an approximately normally distributed predictor X is justified, based on the literature.

The first rows now look like this, yielding 100 rows in the exoData  :
N.per.group <- 20 # balanced group sample sizes
X <- rep(1:5, size = c(.1, .2, .4, .2, .1)*10)
W <- 1:0
designMatrix <- expand.grid(X = X,
                            W = W)

designMatrix$XW <- designMatrix$X * designMatrix$W # interaction
exoData <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:N.per.group, function(i)
  designMatrix))

However, now again I get the a drawParam error:
> sim1 <- sim(nrep = 5000, model = modMed1, covData = exoData, n = nrow(exoData), seed = 777,
+             outfun = rejectMCCI, meanstructure = FALSE)
Progress: 1 / 1
Error in drawParam(model@dgen, maxDraw = maxDraw, numFree = max(model@pt$free),  :
  Cannot obtain valid parameter set within maximum number of draws.

Why is this? Here the part of the code where I used the findFactorResidualVar function:

exoCov <- cov.wt(exoData, method = "ML")$cov

residVar <- findFactorResidualVar(beta = beta.pop, corPsi = diag(2),

                                  gamma = kappa.pop, covcov = exoCov)

(resEq <- binds(free = diag(as.numeric(NA), 2), popParam = diag(residVar)))
diag(residVar)

Thanks everyone for help.
Kindly,
Andi.

Terrence Jorgensen schrieb am Mittwoch, 1. November 2023 um 15:46:01 UTC+1:
> The design matrix calculates the interaction XW prior to setting X's actual (Likert-scale?) values of 1-5. So XW simply = W, which expect would not allow your model to converge because the sample covariance matrix would not be positive definite if 2 predictors are perfectly correlated.
>
> Since you have a Likert-scale predictor, I would recommend you think more carefully about the response distribution you expect (which seems random, not fixed, invalidating the exogeneity assumption of your simulation.)  If you really think that the distribution of X is fixed (i.e., has specific probabilities for each response option), you should first generate a sample of minimal size with that property.  For example, assuming something normalish looking:
>
> (X <- rep(1:5, times = c(.1, .2, .4, .2, .1)*10))
> W <- 1:0
> expand.grid(X, W)
>
> That leads to orthogonal X and W, then you create their interaction term XW.  That basic building block (here, 20 observations) can be repeated however often to yield samples of different sizes following that fixed design (e.g., 5 of those yield N = 100).
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>

messages.subject_clean: Mulit-group SEM, no variance in covariate in one group, how to proceed?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Group,

I try to fit a multigroup SEM in lavaan.

In one of my groups (group 1) all values for a specific covariate are the same (i.e., all students in this group are in grade 5), in my other two groups however this covariate (grade) varies between students. I want to compare other regression coefficients between groups, while controling for the grade in all groups but in group 1. (In other groups 2 and 3 I scale the covariate "grade" as a deviation of grade 5, the level of all students in group 1).

This seems to not be easily possible, lavaan gives the following error message: "lavaan ERROR: some variables have no variance in group 1: grade".

This is my (simplified) model syntax:

    T2   ~ T1 + S1 + grade
    S2   ~ S1 + T1 + grade

    T1   ~~ S1 + grade
    S1   ~~ grade

Can someone give me advice on how to implement my intended analysis?

(I would need an approach that also works for categorical covariates, as the same is also the case for a categorical second covariate "school-type" that varies in groups 2 and 3 but not in group 1)

I would be super happy about advice.

All the Best,

Alex

messages.subject: Re: Mulit-group SEM, no variance in covariate in one group, how to proceed?
messages.subject_clean: Mulit-group SEM, no variance in covariate in one group, how to proceed?
messages.body_plain:
Just being practical, you might replace your actual covariate with another variable which is equal to the real covariate in most groups but is just random noise in the one group. If you leave the covariate's paths fixed at 0 in that one group where your real covariate has no variance, that should address your problem. You could make these random numbers ordinal by using the cut() standard function in R.

messages.body_plain:
I also have the same problem when running a two-level model using MLR estimator in both lavaan and Mplus.

All the test statistics, estimated coefficients, standard errors and p-value are so different. The Chi-square test in lavaan is higher than in M'plus, which indicated better goodness of fit. However, the SRMR within level in lavaan is much higher than in Mplus (0.092 vs 0.010). messages.subject: how to perform contrast tests for pairwise latent correlations in cfa
messages.subject_clean: how to perform contrast tests for pairwise latent correlations in cfa
messages.body_plain:
Dear community,

I am facing a problem writing the correct syntax for a model in which I would like to test whether the latent correlations between one central variable (kind of DV) and several AVs (av1, av2, av3) differ from each other taking into account the dependencies between the avs and the avs with the dv. That is, which of the three correlations (dv~~av1, dv~~av2, dv~~av3) is statistically the strongest/weakest?
The model is as follows (I leave out the measurement model): all variables intercorrelate

#correlations
dv ~~ label1*av1 + label2*av2 + label3*av3

My idea was to use the contrast approach to test all correlation of interest in one model.
First problem: how can I add a label to the dv? Because ist stands on the left side of the equation. Maybe this way?:

#correlations
dv ~~ label1*av1 + label2*av2
av3 ~~ label0*dv
av1 ~~ av2 + av3
av2 ~~ av3

Second: is it correct to form the contrasts this way?

#contrasts
c1 := dv-label1
c2 := dv-label2
c3 := dv-label3

Maybe there is another way that fits better.
Kind regards,
Marcus

Thanks a lot for this suggestion, Edward!

The approach works and parameter estimates are correct (in a model without any constraints across groups, parameter estimates in the single groups are identical to estimates for separate single group models for each of the groups). The only disadvantage is that it impacts the overall fit; I added the smallest random variances I could for the model to still converge (sd=0.01), this lead to the following fit in an otherwise saturated model:

cfi     tli     rmsea    srmr    chsq
1.000   1.027   0.000    0.022   12.291 (2.5% of baseline.chisq)

My conclusion: It is possible to do it as you suggested, but would be easier to report if this workaround would not be necessary.
Do any of you know of other software that may not require this step?

Thanks again and all the Best,
Alex

> based on these produced orthogonal polynomials, we refitted the model as below, and got all estimates normally:
>
> > model_cubic <- '  i =~ 0.4082483*T1 + 0.4082483*T2 + 0.4082483*T3 + 0.4082483*T4 + 0.4082483*T5 + 0.4082483*T6
> s =~ -0.5352015*T1 + -0.3705241*T2 + -0.2058467*T3 + 0.1235080*T4 + 0.3705241*T5 + 0.6175402*T6
> q =~ 0.519842695*T1 + -0.004725843*T2 + -0.353194559*T3 + -0.521832524*T4 + -0.186048965*T5 + 0.545959194*T6
> c =~ -0.4427470*T1 + 0.3554442*T2 + 0.4815676*T3 + -0.2174819*T4 + -0.5258859*T5 + 0.3491029*T6  +  + ' > fit_cubic <- growth(model_cubic, data= data, sampling.weights="WEIGHT2")

That is the same as I would have done, except I just use the contr.poly() function, which gives results for all T-1 polynomials.

contr.poly(1:length(x), scores = x)
             .L           .Q         .C          ^4          ^5
[1,] -0.5352015  0.519842695 -0.4427470  0.24223952 -0.14815996
[2,] -0.3705241 -0.004725843  0.3554442 -0.50228719  0.56337366
[3,] -0.2058467 -0.353194559  0.4815676  0.09658215 -0.65190380
[4,]  0.1235080 -0.521832524 -0.2174819  0.56563215  0.42253024
[5,]  0.3705241 -0.186048965 -0.5258859 -0.57450718 -0.23412931
[6,]  0.6175402  0.545959194  0.3491029  0.17234054  0.04828917

Of course, you don't need to model all higher-order polynomials, but if you do, then you will have a saturated model and can test whether something more complex than cubic is required to fit the data well.

> however, the intercept after using orthogonal polynomials has changed to means across time, which is not what we were expected to explain

I don't know whose expectation you want to meet, but if you want the intercept to be the mean at the first occasion, then you cannot have orthogonal polynomial contrasts.  Contrasts have means of zero by definition, and any pair of contrasts are orthogonal/uncorrelated because their products have means of zero.  Interpreting the usual intercept as "initial status" is just something you give up when you define growth factors as polynomial contrasts.

Voelkle, M. C., & McKnight, P. E. (2012). One size fits all? A Monte-Carlo simulation on the relationship between repeated measures (M)ANOVA and latent curve modeling. Methodology, 8(1), 2338. https://doi.org/10.1027/1614-2241/a000044

The latent "level" or "center-cept" is each person's mean across occasions, so that growth-factor's mean is the grand mean across all occasions and subjects.  Interpreting variability in that quantity is just as valid as interpreting variability in means on the first occasion.

Wainer, H. (2000). The centercept: An estimable and meaningful regression parameter. Psychological Science, 11(5), 434–436. https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-9280.00284

messages.body_plain:
> I also have the same problem when running a two-level model using MLR estimator in both lavaan and Mplus.

If you used the default estimators, they are not the same.  Mplus uses an accelerated EM algorithm to obtain ML estimates, whereas lavaan uses a quasi-Newton algorithm.  Some technical details are provided here:

 https://doi.org/10.3390/psych3020012

kappa.free["Y","X"] <- "c.w0"

kappa.pop["Y","X"] <- c.w0
kappa.pop["Y","W"] <- w.Y

ind.w0 := a.w0 * b
ind.w1 := (a.w0 + a.mod) * b

> can i run a factor analysis for the count data

Using what?  Mplus?  If you have access to that, I'm not sure why you wouldn't fit your full SEM using Mplus.

> to extract the latent variable, and then place the latent variable in regular SEM with the rest of variable being continuous variables?

If you want to trust your SEs, you need to account for the uncertainty about factor-score estimates.  You can obtain "plausible values" using Mplus:

https://statmodel.com/download/Plausible.pdf

> if I can do that, what estimator can I use?

You can use ML(M/R), but you need to use multiple-imputation methods to pool results across plausible values.  You can use semTools for that (see ?runMI).

messages.subject_clean: how to perform contrast tests for pairwise latent correlations in cfa
messages.body_plain:
> is it correct to form the contrasts this way?

No, you labeled the correlations, so define parameters that are pairwise differences between those correlations.

#correlations
dv ~~ label1*av1 + label2*av2 + label3*av3

## differences
corDif_12 := label1 - label2
corDif_13 := label1 - label3
corDif_23 := label2 - label3

Or an omnibus for whether they are all equal can be conducted by comparing this model to one in which the H0 is true (by constraining the 3 correlations to equality):

fit0 <- sem(..., constraints = c("label1 == label2", "label1 == label3"))

Then use lavTestLRT() to compare models.  Or instead of fitting fit0, you can just use a Wald test by passing the same constraints= argument to lavTestWald() with the unconstrained model.

For clarity,  `lavaan.DV=` is NOT an argument from emeans() really, it is from `semTools::emm_basis.lavaan` which has written extensions (`semTools::emm_basis.lavaan` and  semTools::recover_data.lavaan) for lavaan to connect with the emmeans() package. All of this means that it's possible that you should address your question to the author of the `semTools` not emmeans().

Just a quick check, though, is your Covariate1 a binary variable that takes only 0 or 1? If yes, then by default emmeans takes such a binary variable to be a factor not a numeric/continuous variable and likely you don't need to use it in `at=`. see the last example here: https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/semTools/html/lavaan2emmeans.html

> One last question: the p-values are "adjusted" meaning, I can directly compare those against each other within the latent framework?

Adjust for what?  Adjusting for multiple testing (i.e., to maintain a familywise Type I error rate or false-discovery rate) has nothing to do with the latent variable framework.  You can save that subset of parameterEstimates() output and add another column with adjusted p values from p.adjust(). For example:

PE <- parameterEstimates(fit)
PEcor <- PE[PE$op == ":=", ]
PEcor$fdr <- p.adjust(PEcor$pvalue, method = "fdr")

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

That requires a bit of effort.

  First of all, you cannot do a polynomial regression the way you are doing it here. Instead, you should probably use product indicators. See e.g. https://www.mdpi.com/2624-8611/3/3/24

Second, you cannot really do adjusted predictions using latent variable models at all. The idea in adjusted predictions is that you take the observed X variables, calculate changes values of one or more of the observed variables, and calculate predictions based on the model. (For an explanation see  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kddPY0jpMgU&t=287s&pp=ygUUYWRqdXN0ZWQgcHJlZGljdGlvbnM%3D and or page 74 in https://doi.org/10.1177/1094428121991907) This process cannot be applied to latent variables because there are no observed values for X variables and for this reason the margins and prediction package cannot possibly work in this context.

Depending on your expertise, you might be able to calculate a very nice plot using at means prediction and the marginaleffects (https://marginaleffects.com) tidymodels (https://www.tidymodels.org) and ggplot combination (https://ggplot2-book.org)

I use these packages in a paper that I am working on. You can access our code examples here https://osf.io/xp8rf?view_only=5f0d336336044d7289e5b51d4b3d6481. This gets you the plotting but not the latent variable part.

Kelava and Brand explain how to specify a latent variable polynomial regression

Kelava, A., & Brandt, H. (2009). Estimation of nonlinear latent structural equation models using the extended unconstrained approach. Review of Psychology, 16(2), 123-131.

When you put these block together, you should have the plot that you want to have. Unfortunately, I could not find any code examples of this entire process on the internet.

Hope this helps,

Mikko

Dear Mikko!

Yesterday I read all of the interesting papers that you proposed me and I would say that they provided me with a lot of inputs of how to proceed.

Yet, after thinking more I understood that my independent variables X and Y can be treated as observables, since they have only one indicator, instead of two that I thought in the beginning. So, my model in the end looks like this:

Regression:

Reg <- lm(Predicted ~  Xa + Ya + I(Xa^2) + Xa*Ya, data=dat)
library("margins")
library("prediction")
Margins1 <- margins(Reg, at = list(Xa = 5, Ya= 5), vce = "simulation",iterations = 1000)
Point1<-prediction(Reg, at = list(Xa = 5, Ya = 5),type = "response")
summary(Margins1)
summary(Point1)

SEM:

reg <- '
        #measurement
         Predicted =~Z1 + Z2 + Z3

         #path
         Predicted ~  Xa + Ya + I(Xa^2) + Xa*Ya
  '
Reg_fit<- sem(reg, data = dat, estimator = "MLR")

Thus, I do not have interactions between latent factors. I just have a latent factor as outcome variable. So, do you think that there is a way to implement the margins and prediction command that I had when I used regression (in regression I just used the average of the Predicted variable).
In other words, do you think I can do the margins and point estimates in this case and which command or package do you propose?

Best,
John (Yannis)

messages.subject: Re: blavaan, priors
messages.subject_clean: blavaan, priors
messages.body_plain:
Hi Roxanna, from your question I assume that the variable in question you want to set a prior on must have a binomial distribution.

One important thing to understand is that a "prior" is not a parameter (i.e. a single number, like 0.5 in your case) but a probability distribution. That means that what you refer to as 0.5 probably refers to a parameter that defines the density function of that distribution. In the case of a binomial distribution, where the "typical" (used because of its "conjugate" property) prior is a Beta distribution, 0.5 probably refers to the relationship between the alpha and beta parameters (called "mu" in this response <https://stats.stackexchange.com/a/429741>). That would give you a "uniform" (usually understood as "non-informative"*) distribution, but only when alpha = beta = 1. Otherwise, it will give you a symmetric distribution, but the "amount of information" it provides will depend on the actual value of alpha and beta.

I hope this is clear enough, and helpful somehow. In any case, I hate being the one who says it but I think you would need to delve a little deeper into the theory of Bayesian statistical theory to really get an understanding of the topic :)

Daniel

*Please note, terms like "informative" and "information" refer to "how much" previous ("prior") information you want to input into the model, based on your previous assumptions or beliefs, which are based on the prior literature you mention.

--
Daniel Morillo, Ph.D.
GitHub <https://github.com/DaniMori> |  ORCID <https://orcid.org/0000-0003-3021-3878>

messages.subject: Multi-group path analysis - Equality-constrained versus free model
messages.subject_clean: Multi-group path analysis - Equality-constrained versus free model
messages.body_plain:
Hello lavaan group,

I am working on a multi-group path analysis using lavaan (I only have observed variables); however, it has been a challenge to find literature on this. Most of the literature is intended for SEM; however, since I am doing path analysis, there are many steps/considerations that do not apply to path analysis.

I am trying to compare my model across 3 gender groups. Following the literature, I assigned vectors to the parameters to unconstraint them. Looking at the summary, I do see that the estimates vary across groups. However, when I try to compare this unconstrained model with the constrained model (for which I used the argument group.equal = "regressions"), I see exactly the same results in the summary of the constrained and unconstrained group, which seems strange  and makes me think I did something wrong.

Model_de_groups<- '

 ## Direct Paths
  Sense_of_defeat_centered ~ c(a1, a2, a3) * Sense_of_entrapment_centered
  Intention_to_kill_self_centered ~ c(b1, b2, b3) * Sense_of_defeat_centered +
                                     c(d1, d2, d3) * Sense_of_entrapment_centered
  Perceived_capability_for_suicide ~ c(c1, c2, c3) * Intention_to_kill_self_centered

  ##Indirect effects on Perceived_capability_for_suicide for each group
  g1.indirect1 := a1 * b1 * c1    # Group 1
  g2.indirect1 := a2 * b2 * c2    # Group 2
  g3.indirect1 := a3 * b3 * c3    # Group 3

  g1.indirect2 := d1 * c1         # Group 1
  g2.indirect2 := d2 * c2         # Group 2
  g3.indirect2 := d3 * c3         # Group 3

  ## Total effect on Perceived_capability_for_suicide for each group
  g1.total_effect := c1 + g1.indirect1 + g1.indirect2
  g2.total_effect := c2 + g2.indirect1 + g2.indirect2
  g3.total_effect := c3 + g3.indirect1 + g3.indirect2

  ## Variances for each group
  Sense_of_defeat_centered ~~ c(v1, v2, v3) * Sense_of_defeat_centered
  Intention_to_kill_self_centered ~~ c(w1, w2, w3) * Intention_to_kill_self_centered
  Perceived_capability_for_suicide ~~ c(x1, x2, x3) * Perceived_capability_for_suicide

'
#Multigroup

fit.gender.difference= sem(Model_de_groups, data_, estimator = "MLM", group = "Gender")
summary(fit.gender.difference , fit.measures = T, standardized = T)

fit.gender.equal= sem(Model_de_groups, data, estimator = "MLM", group = "Gender", group.equal = "regressions")
summary(fit.gender.equal , fit.measures = T, standardized = T)

Then, when trying to compare the equality-constrained versus the free model, I get this warning:

> Anova_results=anova(fit.gender.difference, fit.gender.equal)

Warning message:
In lavTestLRT(object = object, ..., model.names = NAMES) :
  lavaan WARNING: some models have the same degrees of freedom

Do you have any idea of what I am doing wrong?

Thank you in advance,
Ronald.
_
R. Bahamondes-Álvarez MPhil, MSc | CAD-1 Assistant Coordinator ABO | PhD Candidate in Child and Adolescent Psychiatry - LUMC | Leiden University | Faculty of Social Sciences | Wassenaarseweg 52 | 2333 AK Leiden | The Netherlands

messages.subject: Re: Multi-group path analysis - Equality-constrained versus free model
messages.subject_clean: Multi-group path analysis - Equality-constrained versus free model
messages.body_plain:
You can check the parameter estimates. I guess the regression coefficients are not constrained to be equal even you added group.equal = "regressions" because you used labels on the regression paths (e.g., c(a1, a2, a3)). The argument may not override what you explicitly declare as unconstrained.

To constrain the regression coefficients without writing another version of the model with labels removed, you can manually add the equality constrains this way:

Model_de_groups_eq <- paste(Model_de_groups,
"
a1 == a2
a2 == a3
b1 == b2
b2 == b3
c1 == c2
c2 == c3
d1 == d2
d2 == d3
")

If you fit this model, you should see that the regression paths are constrained between group, with or without group.equal = "regressions".

My two cents.

-- Shu Fai

El mar, 28 nov 2023 a las 10:51, Dessalegn Kiross (<dessa...@gmail.com>) escribió:

>  Kindly answer the following questions by looking at the r-output
> 1. is it ok that standard errors of the residuals and intercepts are not reported, but the factor variance errors are reported

Totally ok. The residuals are identified by the "scale" (see answer to 3) and the factor loadings, so they are not actually estimated, neither are the intercepts as they would not be identified.

> 2. the p.value for the variance of factor 2 is not significant, does this mean I have to drop this specific factor

You can try and then run a likelihood ratio test between the two models. If you lose fit you have evidence that factor 2 is actually necessary to have a good model fit. Nevertheless, I'd argue that it is also important to take into account theoretical aspects when making that decision.

> 3. what do the scales y* indicate

That is the variance of the "latent utility". This implies that the variance resulting from summing up the effect of all the factors + the uniqueness of the items is fixed to 1 for all of them. Similarly, the intercepts, fixed to 0, are interpreted as the mean of the distribution of that same latent utility. These two constraints (for each item) are necessary for interpretation.

> 4. Model fit indices are many: there are scaled, standard, and robust. which fit indices should I use

Although I'm sure you'll receive better suggestions, you need to consider at least CFI, TLI, (robust) RMSEA, and SRMR.

> 5. anything that you think would help improve the scale, recommendations or changes should I make

I'd only try to fix the variances of the factors to 1 and free the loadings of the first item for each latent factor. Although it's a matter of preference, I find it easier to understand in the case of latent variable modeling with ordinal indicators, such as your case.

Hope it helps!
--
Daniel Morillo, Ph.D.
GitHub <https://github.com/DaniMori> |  ORCID <https://orcid.org/0000-0003-3021-3878>

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am trying to cross-validate a multi-group sem with ordered categorical variables using k-fold cross-validation. The idea is to train a model in the k-fold cross-validation, then extract the parameter estimates from the final model and fit it to the data in the holdout sample. I want to use the likelihood to see if the fit is better, worse or similar between the training and the holdout data. Without more details on the k-fold CV I am running into a problem when "fitting" the model to the holdout.

I have extracted the parameter estimates from the final model of the k-fold CV. Now,  I want to evaluate the fit of these parameter estimates in my holdout sample (to the data) to account for the out of sample prediction error. Basically, I was thinking of "fitting" the model without estimating it. Hence, using the extracted parameter estimates as starting values and setting them as fixed.

I am not sure I achieve this with the code below. I am fairly new to sem and lavaan and happy to answer questions.  I am also wondering if the chi square in this instance is a good choice to see the fit or if extracting the DWLS value would be better.

library(lavaan)
fit_part_resid_eval <- cfa(pt_part_resid,
# parameter estimates from the model trained in the k-fold cross validation
                           data = holdout_df,
                           ordered = c("item1","item2", .... "item 25"), # 25 items, ordered
                           group = "age_cat", group.label=c("1", "2", "3","4"), # group variable age groups
                           estimator = "DWLS",
                           test = "scaled.shifted",
                           se = "robust",
                           parameterization = "theta",
                           control = list(optim.method="none", optim.force.converged=TRUE)
# with this I am trying to force lavaan to only fit and not estimate.
                           )

rejectMCCI <- function(object) {
  CIs <- semTools::monteCarloCI(object)
  apply(CIs, margin = 1, function(CI) 0 < CI["ci.lower"] | 0 > CI["ci.upper"] )
}

N.per.group <- 50 # balanced group sample sizes

X <- rep(1:5, size = c(.1, .2, .4, .2, .1)*10)
W <- 1:0
designMatrix <- expand.grid(X = X,
                            W = W)
designMatrix$XW <- designMatrix$X * designMatrix$W # interaction
exoData <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:N.per.group, function(i)
  designMatrix))

a.w0 <- .5 # effect of X on M when moderator (W) == 0
a.mod <- .3 # how much “a” path is moderated by W (i.e., interaction)
b.w0 <- .4 # effect of M on Y when moderator (W) == 0
b.mod <- 0 # no moderating effect on “b” path
c.w0 <-.2 # effect of X on Y when moderator (W) == 0
c.mod <- 0 # no moderating effect on “c” path
w.M <- .2 # simple effect of moderator (W) on M when X == 0
w.Y <- .2 # simple effect of moderator (W) on Y when X == 0
kappa.free <- kappa.pop <- matrix(NA, # estimate all effects
                                     nrow = 2, # 2 outcomes (M and Y)
                                     ncol = 3, # dummy coded X, W, XW
                                     dimnames = list(c("M", "Y"),names(exoData)))
kappa.free["M","X"] <- "a.w0" # label free parameters
kappa.free["M","W"] <- 0 # (to define indirect effects)
kappa.free["M","XW"] <- "a.mod"
kappa.free["Y","X"] <- "c.w0"
kappa.free["Y","W"] <- 0
kappa.free["Y","XW"] <- 0 # fixed to 0; label “c.mod” to free
kappa.pop["M","X"] <- a.w0 # set population parameters
kappa.pop["M","W"] <- w.M # (defined above)
kappa.pop["M","XW"] <- a.mod
kappa.pop["Y","X"] <- c.w0
kappa.pop["Y","W"] <- w.Y
kappa.pop["Y","XW"] <- c.mod
exoPaths <- bind(free = kappa.free, popParam = kappa.pop)
beta.free <- beta.pop <- matrix(0, nrow = 2, ncol = 2,
                                   dimnames = list(c("M","Y"), c("M","Y")))
beta.free["Y","M"] <- "b"
beta.pop["Y","M"] <- b.w0
endoPaths <- bind(free = beta.free, popParam = beta.pop)
exoCov <- cov.wt(exoData, method = "ML")$cov
residVar <- findFactorResidualVar(beta = beta.pop, corPsi = diag(2),
                                  gamma = kappa.pop, covcov = exoCov)

(diag(residVar))
resEq <- binds(free = diag(as.numeric(NA), 2), popParam = diag(residVar))

userParams <- '
ind.w0 := a.w0 * b
ind.w1 := (a.w0 + a.mod) * b
ind.diff := a.mod * b

'

modMed1 <- model.path(BE = endoPaths,  PS = resEq,

                         KA = exoPaths, con = userParams,
                         indLab = rownames(kappa.free),
                         covLab = colnames(kappa.free))

sim1 <- sim(nrep = 5000, model = modMed1, covData = exoData, n = nrow(exoData), seed = 1027,

            outfun = rejectMCCI, meanstructure = FALSE)

summaryParam(sim1, matchParam = TRUE, digits = 3)
testMCCI <- do.call(rbind, getExtraOutput(sim1))
colMeans(testMCCI)

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Quick questions on how I should handle non-normal data in lavaan.

Usually, I would run the model using code similar to what can be found below. From my understanding this is asking lavaan to bootstrap the standard errors
fNM.NR.PATH  <- sem(NM.NR.PATH ,data=D_, se="boot", bootstrap=2000)

However, from my understanding, running the model with maximum likelihood estimation with robust standard errors and ﻿Satorra-Bentler scaled test-statistic is appropriate given my data is a bit skewed. Therefore, this is the code I used:
fNM.NR.PATH  <- sem(NM.NR.PATH ,data=D_, se="robust.sem", estimator = 'MLM', bootstrap=2000)

My questions are:
1. Did I use the right code given the non-normality of my data?

2. When I ran the code using se="robust.sem", estimator = 'MLM', bootstrap=2000, lavaan immediately printed out my results. Typically when I use bootstraps in a large sample (N = 302), lavaan takes at least a few seconds (if not minutes) to complete the analysis.

 Additionally, when using bootstraps, I usually see this printed in my summary output:  "Number of requested bootstrap draws=2000, Number of successful bootstrap draws  =2000". However in this case, this was not included in my output.

Thus I am wondering, did lavaan actually perform any bootstrapping?

Thanks!
Nick

messages.subject: Re: Replications not convergent
messages.subject_clean: Replications not convergent
messages.body_plain:
Thank you for the reprex.  As I pointed out before, your mediator's residual variance is negative, so your effects are too big to be interpreted in units of SD, i.e., your explained variance is > 1.

If I simply lower your moderator's effect to a.mod <- .2,  the simulation works fine, after also changing some typos.  Bear in mind that R is case-sensitive:
In the sim() function, the argument is nRep= not nrep=
In your rejectMCCI() function definition, the apply() function's second argument is MARGIN= not margin=
5000 reps is not necessary to demonstrate the issue, so I just run 5 reps in the reprex below:

library(simsem)

rejectMCCI <- function(object) {
  CIs <- semTools::monteCarloCI(object)

  apply(CIs, MARGIN = 1, function(CI) 0 < CI["ci.lower"] | 0 > CI["ci.upper"] )

}

N.per.group <- 50 # balanced group sample sizes

X <- rep(1:5, size = c(.1, .2, .4, .2, .1)*10)
W <- 1:0
designMatrix <- expand.grid(X = X, W = W)
designMatrix$XW <- designMatrix$X * designMatrix$W # interaction
exoData <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:N.per.group, function(i) designMatrix))

a.w0 <- .5 # effect of X on M when moderator (W) == 0

a.mod <- .2 # how much “a” path is moderated by W (i.e., interaction)

b.w0 <- .4 # effect of M on Y when moderator (W) == 0
b.mod <- 0 # no moderating effect on “b” path
c.w0 <-.2 # effect of X on Y when moderator (W) == 0
c.mod <- 0 # no moderating effect on “c” path
w.M <- .2 # simple effect of moderator (W) on M when X == 0
w.Y <- .2 # simple effect of moderator (W) on Y when X == 0
kappa.free <- kappa.pop <- matrix(NA, # estimate all effects
                                  nrow = 2, # 2 outcomes (M and Y)
                                  ncol = 3, # dummy coded X, W, XW
                                  dimnames = list(c("M", "Y"),names(exoData)))
kappa.free["M","X"] <- "a.w0" # label free parameters
kappa.free["M","W"] <- 0 # (to define indirect effects)
kappa.free["M","XW"] <- "a.mod"
kappa.free["Y","X"] <- "c.w0"
kappa.free["Y","W"] <- 0
kappa.free["Y","XW"] <- 0 # fixed to 0; label “c.mod” to free
kappa.pop["M","X"] <- a.w0 # set population parameters
kappa.pop["M","W"] <- w.M # (defined above)
kappa.pop["M","XW"] <- a.mod
kappa.pop["Y","X"] <- c.w0
kappa.pop["Y","W"] <- w.Y
kappa.pop["Y","XW"] <- c.mod
exoPaths <- bind(free = kappa.free, popParam = kappa.pop)
beta.free <- beta.pop <- matrix(0, nrow = 2, ncol = 2,
                                dimnames = list(c("M","Y"), c("M","Y")))
beta.free["Y","M"] <- "b"
beta.pop["Y","M"] <- b.w0
endoPaths <- bind(free = beta.free, popParam = beta.pop)
exoCov <- cov.wt(exoData, method = "ML")$cov
residVar <- findFactorResidualVar(beta = beta.pop, corPsi = diag(2),
                                  gamma = kappa.pop, covcov = exoCov)

(diag(residVar))
resEq <- binds(free = diag(as.numeric(NA), 2), popParam = diag(residVar))

userParams <- '
ind.w0 := a.w0 * b
ind.w1 := (a.w0 + a.mod) * b
ind.diff := a.mod * b
'

modMed1 <- model.path(BE = endoPaths,  PS = resEq,
                      KA = exoPaths, con = userParams,
                      indLab = rownames(kappa.free),
                      covLab = colnames(kappa.free))

sim1 <- sim(nRep = 5, model = modMed1, covData = exoData, n = nrow(exoData), seed = 1027,

            outfun = rejectMCCI, meanstructure = FALSE)

summaryParam(sim1, matchParam = TRUE, digits = 3, detail = T)

testMCCI <- do.call(rbind, getExtraOutput(sim1))
colMeans(testMCCI)

While working on this example, I found a bug that mistakenly transformed what getExtraOutput() should return.  So you can install the latest development version (0.5-16.911) again before running it with many replications.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
Thank you Daniel for the helpful feedback,

On Tue, Nov 28, 2023 at 11:44 PM Daniel Morillo Cuadrado <danielmo...@gmail.com> wrote:

> El mar, 28 nov 2023 a las 10:51, Dessalegn Kiross (<dessa...@gmail.com>) escribió:
> >  Kindly answer the following questions by looking at the r-output
> > 1. is it ok that standard errors of the residuals and intercepts are not reported, but the factor variance errors are reported
>
> Totally ok. The residuals are identified by the "scale" (see answer to 3) and the factor loadings, so they are not actually estimated, neither are the intercepts as they would not be identified.
>
> > 2. the p.value for the variance of factor 2 is not significant, does this mean I have to drop this specific factor
>
> You can try and then run a likelihood ratio test between the two models. If you lose fit you have evidence that factor 2 is actually necessary to have a good model fit. Nevertheless, I'd argue that it is also important to take into account theoretical aspects when making that decision.
>
> > 3. what do the scales y* indicate
>
> That is the variance of the "latent utility". This implies that the variance resulting from summing up the effect of all the factors + the uniqueness of the items is fixed to 1 for all of them. Similarly, the intercepts, fixed to 0, are interpreted as the mean of the distribution of that same latent utility. These two constraints (for each item) are necessary for interpretation.
>
> > 4. Model fit indices are many: there are scaled, standard, and robust. which fit indices should I use
>
> Although I'm sure you'll receive better suggestions, you need to consider at least CFI, TLI, (robust) RMSEA, and SRMR.
>
> > 5. anything that you think would help improve the scale, recommendations or changes should I make
>
> I'd only try to fix the variances of the factors to 1 and free the loadings of the first item for each latent factor. Although it's a matter of preference, I find it easier to understand in the case of latent variable modeling with ordinal indicators, such as your case.
>
> Hope it helps!
